summary: The note examines the history of pesticide use in local agriculture and its growing risks to terrestrial and aquatic wildlife, from DDT through neonicotinoids and atrazine. It cites local experts, a bee-decline study, and a Spring River contamination finding. It also covers Integrated Pest Management, a new monitoring program, and community calls for stricter controls.
one_line: Overview of how local agricultural pesticide use, from DDT to neonicotinoids and atrazine, harms bees, fish and amphibians, and of emerging alternatives and policy responses.
key_facts: Rachel Carson's "Silent Spring" (1962) made the public aware of the environmental hazards of chemical pesticides such as DDT.
Dr. Jane Bell, an ecologist and professor at the local university, said in a September 5, 2023 interview that early pesticide use was undertaken "with little regard for the ecological consequences."
After DDT was banned, organophosphates, carbamates and pyrethroids were developed in the 1970s and 1980s, and they are still in use today.
Neonicotinoids, insecticides used locally since the late 1990s, have been implicated in the decline of pollinators like bees and butterflies.
A study released October 10, 2023 by the Local Environmental Research Institute found a marked decline in local bee populations coinciding with intensified neonicotinoid use on nearby farms.

Dr. Emily Clark, lead researcher at the Local Environmental Research Institute, said the correlation suggests a strong impact on pollinators with possible cascading effects on plant pollination and ecosystem health.
On September 15, 2023, an investigation found pesticide levels exceeding safe limits in the local Spring River.
The Spring River report highlighted atrazine, a herbicide commonly used in corn production, at concentrations known to disrupt the endocrine systems of fish and amphibians.
Runoff from agricultural fields carries pesticides into waterways, causing altered growth, reproductive failure and mortality in fish, amphibia and invertebrates.
Farmer John Doe, whose family has farmed local land since the 1950s, has begun using Integrated Pest Management, including crop rotations, cover crops and natural predators.
The Local Environmental Agency announced a Pesticide Impact Assessment Program on November 2, 2023 to monitor long-term effects of agricultural chemicals on non-target species.
A town hall meeting on December 12, 2023 brought together policy experts, farmers and residents to discuss the future of local agriculture and pesticide controls.
